title: Lesson 7: Understanding the Difference Between Correction and Personal Attack
summary: Legitimate feedback is not automatically an attack. Insults, humiliation and degrading remarks are not correction.

items.label: Duration
items.body: 45–60 minutes

items.label: Participants
items.body: All Zura Spa staff

items.label: Focus
items.body: Emotional intelligence, understanding feedback, professional boundaries, respectful communication and workplace accountability

sections.title: 1. Introduction
paragraphs: Imagine a therapist at Zura Spa finishes a massage session and forgets to replenish the treatment-room supplies.
Her supervisor notices and says: "Please ensure you replenish the supplies after every session so the next therapist can prepare without delays."

The therapist becomes upset. She thinks: "Why does she always have something to say about my work? Does she think I'm incompetent? Why is she attacking me?" She responds angrily: "Why are you always finding fault with me? I'm not the only person working here!"
What began as a straightforward correction has now become an argument.

But consider another situation. A supervisor says to an employee: "You're so useless. I don't understand why we employed someone who cannot do simple things properly." The employee feels embarrassed and hurt.
This time, the problem is not merely that the employee dislikes being corrected. The supervisor has used degrading language that attacks the employee's dignity.

These situations are different. In the first example, the supervisor identified a work-related issue and requested improvement. In the second, the supervisor insulted the employee rather than focusing on the work.
One is correction. The other is a personal attack.
At Zura Spa, employees must learn to recognise this difference.
Employees should not automatically interpret every correction as an attack. Equally, supervisors and colleagues should not disguise insults, intimidation or humiliation as correction.
A professional workplace requires both the willingness to receive legitimate feedback and the responsibility to communicate it respectfully.

sections.title: 2. What is correction?
paragraphs: Correction is feedback or guidance intended to address a mistake, improve behaviour, clarify expectations or maintain an appropriate standard.
Constructive correction generally focuses on something specific that a person did or failed to do.
Correction may be uncomfortable, especially when the employee knows a mistake was made. However, discomfort alone does not make feedback a personal attack.
Correction addresses an action, decision, behaviour or result that needs improvement.
list: "Please confirm the client's appointment time before completing the booking."
"The treatment room was not fully prepared. Ensure the towels and supplies are ready before the next session."
"The client requested lighter pressure. Please adjust the massage accordingly."
"You arrived after your scheduled start time. Please ensure you are ready to begin work on time."
"The maintenance concern was not reported. Please escalate such issues promptly."

sections.title: 3. What is a personal attack?
paragraphs: A personal attack occurs when communication targets someone's dignity, character, identity or personal worth through insults, ridicule, degrading remarks or other inappropriate behaviour rather than addressing the relevant issue constructively.
Such statements do not clearly explain the mistake or provide useful guidance. They focus on degrading the individual.
A personal attack may also involve repeated mockery, public humiliation, threats or offensive comments about someone's personal characteristics.
An employee's mistake may require correction, but it does not remove the employee's right to dignity and respect.
list: "You are useless."
"You have no sense."
"You're too stupid to understand."
"Nobody likes working with you."
"You will never amount to anything."
"You're an embarrassment to this team."

sections.title: 4. Key differences between correction and personal attack
paragraphs: A correction can be firm, direct and serious without being a personal attack.
table: Addresses a specific issue
Targets the person's worth or character
Focuses on behaviour or performance
Uses insults or degrading labels
Explains what needs improvement
May offer no practical guidance
Uses professional language
Uses hostile or humiliating language
Allows questions and clarification
May silence or intimidate the person
Is based on relevant facts
May rely on exaggeration or accusations
Seeks a better outcome
May seek to shame or hurt
Can be firm without being abusive
May involve mockery, threats or intimidation

sections.title: Important distinction
paragraphs: For example: "This is the third time the booking confirmation procedure has not been followed. We need to address the repeated errors and agree on an improvement plan." This is a serious correction, but it focuses on documented work-related concerns.
By contrast: "You are completely useless. You never do anything right." This is degrading and provides no constructive direction.

sections.title: 5. Why employees sometimes interpret correction as a personal attack
paragraphs: Understanding these factors helps employees reflect on their reactions without dismissing genuine concerns about inappropriate treatment.

items.label: 1. Emotional sensitivity
items.body: An employee may feel hurt or embarrassed when a mistake is identified.

items.label: 2. Fear of blame
items.body: The employee may worry that correction will lead to punishment or loss of trust.

items.label: 3. Personal pride
items.body: Some employees find it difficult to accept that their work may need improvement.

items.label: 4. Previous experiences
items.body: Past experiences of harsh criticism or humiliation may influence how feedback is interpreted.

items.label: 5. Perceived unfairness
items.body: An employee may believe she is being singled out or blamed for something outside her responsibility.

items.label: 6. Misunderstanding
items.body: Tone, incomplete information or unclear instructions may cause an employee to misunderstand the intention of the feedback.

sections.title: 6. Feeling hurt does not automatically mean you were attacked
paragraphs: Feedback can be uncomfortable even when it is fair and respectful.
An employee may feel embarrassed because a mistake was noticed. She may feel disappointed because she worked hard. She may feel frustrated because she believes others make similar mistakes.
These feelings are real. However, the employee should examine what was actually said and done before deciding whether the communication was a personal attack.
Your feelings deserve attention, but the facts also matter.

sections.title: Example — a punctuality reminder
paragraphs: A supervisor says: "You arrived 15 minutes after your scheduled start time today. Please ensure you are punctual."
The employee feels embarrassed. However, the statement identifies a specific issue and communicates an expectation.

sections.title: A useful self-check
list: Did the person identify a work-related concern?
Did they attack my character or personal worth?
Was the statement factual?
Was the language respectful?
Was there a clear expectation or requested improvement?
Am I reacting mainly to the words used or to how uncomfortable I feel?

sections.title: 7. Not every harsh tone is a personal attack
paragraphs: Tone matters in workplace communication.
However, it is important to distinguish between a firm instruction, an unnecessarily harsh delivery and an actual personal attack.
A correction does not become abusive simply because it is firm. However, a legitimate concern does not justify insults, threats or humiliation.
Both the content and the manner of communication should be considered.

items.label: Example A: Firm correction
items.body: "Stop using that equipment immediately. It is unsafe." The instruction is direct and urgent. It may be necessary to protect someone from harm.

items.label: Example B: Unnecessarily harsh correction
items.body: "I've told you several times to check that equipment. Why is this still happening?" The tone may be frustrated, but the statement remains focused on the issue. The supervisor may need to communicate more constructively, and the employee may need to address the repeated concern.

items.label: Example C: Personal attack
items.body: "You're an idiot. Only someone without sense would make that mistake." This is an insult directed at the person.

sections.title: 8. The difference between criticism of behaviour and criticism of character
paragraphs: This distinction is central to the lesson.
When correcting someone, describe what happened, what standard or expectation applies, why the issue matters and what should happen differently.
Avoid making sweeping judgments about the person's identity or worth.

items.label: Behaviour-focused correction
items.body: "You interrupted your colleague several times during the discussion." This identifies an observable behaviour.

items.label: Character attack
items.body: "You are a disrespectful and terrible person." This labels the individual's character.

items.label: Behaviour-focused
items.body: "The client was not informed about the appointment delay."

items.label: Character-focused
items.body: "You don't care about clients." This assumes a negative personal quality rather than addressing the specific failure.

sections.title: 9. The FACT method for evaluating correction

items.label: F — Focus on what was said
items.body: Consider the actual words and behaviour rather than immediately assuming the person's intention.

items.label: A — Assess the issue
items.body: Determine whether there is a genuine work-related concern requiring attention.

items.label: C — Consider the communication
items.body: Evaluate the language, tone, context and whether the person used insults or degrading behaviour.

items.label: T — Take an appropriate step
items.body: Accept valid correction, seek clarification, request respectful communication or report serious concerns as appropriate.

sections.title: FACT example
paragraphs: A supervisor says: "The booking was entered incorrectly. Please verify the appointment details before confirming future bookings."
The employee applies FACT. She identifies the actual statement, considers the booking error, recognises that no personal insult was made and responds professionally.
If the booking information is incorrect, she can clarify the facts respectfully.

sections.title: 10. How to respond when the feedback is constructive
paragraphs: When a correction is legitimate and respectfully communicated, employees should focus on understanding and improvement.
The employee does not need to defend her entire professional identity because of one mistake.

items.label: Step 1: Listen
items.body: Allow the person to finish explaining the concern.

items.label: Step 2: Clarify
items.body: Ask questions if the issue is unclear.

items.label: Step 3: Acknowledge valid points
items.body: Accept responsibility where appropriate.

items.label: Step 4: Explain relevant circumstances
items.body: Provide important facts without unnecessary blame-shifting.

items.label: Step 5: Take corrective action
items.body: Address the issue and improve the relevant work habit.

sections.title: Example — missing clean towels
paragraphs: A supervisor says: "The treatment room was missing clean towels before the appointment."
Professional response: "I understand. I overlooked the towel check. I'm sorry. I'll correct it now and ensure I complete the room preparation before the next session."

sections.title: 11. How to respond when correction becomes a personal attack
paragraphs: Employees should not respond to insults with further insults.
However, they are entitled to request respectful communication and report inappropriate behaviour.
Professionalism does not require an employee to remain in an abusive or threatening interaction.

sections.title: Example — an insulting colleague
paragraphs: A colleague says: "You're so stupid. You can't even complete a simple task."
Professional boundary-setting response: "I understand there may be a concern about the task, and I'm willing to discuss it. However, please address the issue without insulting me."
If the behaviour continues: "I would prefer that we involve the supervisor so we can resolve this appropriately."

sections.title: Appropriate responses may include
list: Requesting that the conversation remain respectful.
Asking to discuss the issue privately.
Taking a brief pause when safe and appropriate.
Recording relevant details of serious or repeated incidents.
Reporting threats, harassment or persistent humiliation through the appropriate channel.

sections.title: 12. Correction from a supervisor versus personal attack from a supervisor
paragraphs: Supervisors have responsibility for maintaining work standards. This may include giving difficult feedback, addressing repeated mistakes and communicating performance expectations.
However, supervisory authority does not justify abusive communication.
Respect must operate in both directions.

items.label: Appropriate supervisory correction
items.body: "You have arrived late three times this week. We need to discuss your punctuality and how to ensure your scheduled start time is met."

items.label: Inappropriate personal attack
items.body: "You're useless and unreliable. I don't know why you're still employed here."

sections.title: Supervisor responsibilities
list: Communicate expectations clearly.
Address specific behaviour.
Base feedback on accurate information.
Allow employees to explain relevant circumstances.
Avoid insults and humiliation.
Apply standards fairly.
Follow appropriate reporting and disciplinary procedures.

sections.title: Employee responsibilities
list: Listen to legitimate feedback.
Avoid unnecessary hostility.
Explain relevant facts.
Accept genuine responsibility.
Follow reasonable instructions.
Report inappropriate treatment through appropriate channels.

sections.title: 13. Correction from colleagues versus personal attack from colleagues
paragraphs: Colleagues may raise work-related concerns when shared responsibilities are affected.
However, colleagues should not use feedback to dominate, ridicule or intimidate one another.
If a colleague repeatedly ignores legitimate concerns, the appropriate response is to involve the designated supervisor rather than escalate the situation through insults or retaliation.

sections.title: Example — unreplenished supplies
paragraphs: A therapist notices that another therapist has not replenished the room supplies.
Appropriate correction: "The massage oil wasn't replenished after the previous session. Please, can we ensure it is checked before the room is handed over?"
Personal attack: "You're so lazy. Everyone knows you're the problem here."
The first statement addresses a practical concern. The second makes a degrading judgment about the employee.

sections.title: 14. When repeated correction feels like targeting
paragraphs: An employee may feel targeted when the same issue is raised repeatedly.
However, repeated correction is not automatically unfair.
The important questions are whether the concern is genuine, the expectations are reasonable and the employee is being treated fairly.
Repeated correction should be evaluated based on fairness, facts, consistency and communication—not frequency alone.

items.label: Situation A: Legitimate repeated correction
items.body: An employee repeatedly fails to complete the room-preparation checklist. The supervisor has explained the requirement several times, but the issue continues. Further correction may be appropriate.

items.label: Situation B: Potentially unfair treatment
items.body: A supervisor repeatedly criticises one employee for minor issues while ignoring the same conduct by others, uses insulting language and makes humiliating remarks. This may raise concerns about inconsistent or inappropriate treatment.

sections.title: What should the employee do?
list: Identify the specific concerns being raised.
Review whether the feedback is accurate.
Ask for clear expectations.
Keep relevant records where appropriate.
Raise concerns about inconsistent treatment respectfully.
Use an appropriate escalation channel if the situation continues.

sections.title: 15. When correction is accurate but the delivery is inappropriate
paragraphs: Sometimes a person may raise a valid concern in an inappropriate way.
For example, a therapist genuinely failed to prepare a room, but the supervisor publicly insults her.
Two issues exist: the employee's failure to prepare the room, and the supervisor's inappropriate communication. Both can be addressed.
Professional response: "I understand that the room was not prepared correctly, and I'll address that. However, I would appreciate discussing the matter without personal insults."
An employee's mistake does not excuse abusive correction. Likewise, inappropriate delivery does not automatically remove the employee's responsibility for a genuine work-related mistake.
Two things can be true at the same time: the correction may be valid, and the way it was delivered may be wrong.

sections.title: 16. How to avoid turning your own correction into a personal attack
paragraphs: Every employee should apply the same standard when correcting others.
list: Am I addressing a genuine work-related issue?
Do I know the relevant facts?
Am I about to criticise the behaviour or the person's identity?
Am I using language I would consider respectful if directed at me?
Is this the appropriate setting?
What practical improvement do I want?

sections.title: Example — an appointment change
paragraphs: Personal attack: "You are so irresponsible. You never think about anyone else."
Constructive correction: "The appointment change wasn't communicated, and this affected the therapist's preparation. Please ensure future changes are passed on promptly."
The second statement is more useful because it explains the problem and expected improvement.

sections.title: 17. Personal boundaries and reporting serious concerns
paragraphs: Employees should understand that some workplace conduct requires more than a polite request for better communication.
Such conduct should not be dismissed as ordinary correction.
Employees should seek assistance through appropriate supervisory or management channels, and use other applicable reporting or emergency channels where necessary.
When the person involved is the employee's direct supervisor, the employee should be able to raise the matter with another appropriate authority.
Maintaining a respectful workplace requires accountability for both work performance and interpersonal conduct.
list: Threats of violence.
Sexual harassment.
Discriminatory insults.
Repeated intimidation.
Deliberate humiliation.
Retaliation after reporting concerns.
Coercion or threats intended to silence an employee.

sections.title: Case study A: The offended therapist
paragraphs: A supervisor tells a therapist: "Please ensure the massage oil is replenished after every session." The therapist becomes upset and says: "Why are you always attacking me?"
Expected lesson: Feeling uncomfortable does not automatically make legitimate feedback a personal attack.
list: Was the supervisor's statement a personal attack?
Why might the therapist feel offended?
How should the therapist evaluate the correction?
What would be a professional response?
What improvement is required?

sections.title: Case study B: The insulting supervisor
paragraphs: A receptionist enters an appointment incorrectly. The supervisor says: "You're so stupid. You can't even handle a simple booking."
Expected lesson: A genuine mistake does not justify insults or degrading communication.
list: Was there a legitimate work-related concern?
What made the communication a personal attack?
How could the supervisor correct the mistake respectfully?
How should the receptionist respond?
What should happen if this behaviour is repeated?

sections.title: Case study C: The repeated correction
paragraphs: A therapist has been reminded several times to complete the room checklist. She feels the supervisor is deliberately targeting her. However, the records show that the checklist has repeatedly been left incomplete.
Expected lesson: Repeated feedback may be appropriate when a genuine performance issue remains unresolved.
list: Does repeated correction automatically mean unfair treatment?
What facts should be considered?
What responsibility belongs to the therapist?
How can the supervisor make expectations clear?
What practical improvement plan would help?

sections.title: Case study D: The unfair accusation
paragraphs: A therapist is accused of leaving a room untidy. She explains that the room was used again after she completed her preparation. The supervisor checks the information and discovers that the original accusation was incorrect.
Expected lesson: Fair correction requires accurate information and a willingness to revise conclusions.
list: Was the correction based on accurate information?
How should the therapist explain her perspective?
What should the supervisor do after discovering the mistake?
How can the team prevent similar misunderstandings?

sections.title: 19. Practical group activity: Correction or personal attack?
paragraphs: Activity duration: 10 minutes.
Purpose: Help employees distinguish constructive correction from degrading communication.
The trainer should read each statement aloud. Participants should identify whether it is constructive correction, inappropriate communication or a personal attack.

Follow-up role-play: Choose two statements classified as personal attacks and rewrite them as constructive feedback. Participants should practise delivering the revised feedback using a respectful tone and clear expectations.

items.label: 1. "Please ensure the room checklist is completed before the next appointment."
items.body: Constructive correction.

items.label: 2. "You're useless. You never do anything right."
items.body: Personal attack.

items.label: 3. "This is the third booking error this week. We need to review the process and prevent further mistakes."
items.body: Constructive correction — firm and serious, still focused on the work.

items.label: 4. "Can't you use your brain for once?"
items.body: Personal attack.

items.label: 5. "You didn't inform the therapist about the schedule change. What happened?"
items.body: Constructive correction.

items.label: 6. "The task was not completed, but the supervisor shouts about it in front of clients."
items.body: Inappropriate communication — the concern may be valid, but the delivery is not.

sections.title: 20. Interactive assessment
paragraphs: Complete the Lesson 7 Knowledge Check at the bottom of this lesson. Choose an option, give your reason, then submit.
list: What is the main difference between correction and a personal attack? Correction is always pleasant, while personal attacks are always loud / Correction addresses behaviour or performance, while personal attacks degrade the person / Correction can only come from management

A supervisor says, "You arrived late today. Please ensure you are punctual." What is this? A work-related correction / Automatically a personal attack / Harassment simply because it feels uncomfortable
Which statement is clearly a personal attack? Please complete the room checklist. / The booking was entered incorrectly. / You are useless and have no sense.

What should an employee do if feedback is valid but delivered with insults? Ignore the work-related issue entirely / Address the genuine concern and raise the inappropriate communication respectfully / Respond with stronger insults

What does the FACT method encourage? Focusing on the words, assessing the issue, considering communication and taking an appropriate step / Finding someone else to blame / Assuming every correction is an attack

sections.title: 21. Personal assignment
paragraphs: Each employee should answer the following questions in writing.
list: Explain what constructive correction means.
Define a personal attack and give three workplace examples.
Identify five differences between correction and personal attack.
Explain why an employee may feel offended even when feedback is legitimate.
Describe the difference between a firm instruction and an insulting statement.
Explain the FACT method in your own words.
Describe how you would respond if a supervisor corrected you respectfully for a genuine mistake.
Explain how you would respond if a colleague insulted you while raising a work-related concern.
Describe why repeated correction does not automatically mean an employee is being targeted.
Explain what should happen when a correction is valid but the language used is inappropriate.
Identify three ways you can ensure that your own feedback never becomes a personal attack.

sections.title: 22. Seven-day practical challenge
table: Pay attention to the difference between feedback and personal insults
Avoid automatically interpreting correction as rejection
Practise separating work-related behaviour from personal identity
Apply the FACT method when receiving feedback
Give a colleague constructive feedback without attacking their character
Practise setting respectful boundaries when communication becomes inappropriate
Reflect on how your understanding of correction has improved

sections.title: 23. Final lesson and takeaway
paragraphs: Correction is a necessary part of learning, teamwork and maintaining professional standards.
However, correction and personal attacks are not the same.
At Zura Spa, employees should be willing to receive legitimate feedback without automatically interpreting it as hostility or rejection.
At the same time, supervisors and colleagues must communicate corrections without insults, humiliation, intimidation or personal attacks.
Employees should evaluate feedback based on facts, language, context and the improvement being requested.
They should accept genuine responsibility, clarify inaccurate information respectfully and report inappropriate conduct through the proper channels.
Next module: Day 5 — Conflict Resolution and Handling Difficult Situations.

remember: Not every correction is an attack, and not every uncomfortable conversation is disrespectful. Sometimes, feedback simply reveals an area where you need to improve. At the same time, no mistake makes you deserving of insults or humiliation. At Zura Spa, we value a workplace where people can be corrected without being degraded, where employees can learn without becoming hostile, and where respect and accountability work together to build a stronger team.
